passage:
Monday. At lunch, Jatin opened the class chat and found a photo of himself mid-stumble on sports day, with cruel comments under it. His hands went cold and he wanted to disappear. He did not reply. He took screenshots of the photo and the names, then put the phone away.
Tuesday. Still feeling sick, Jatin walked into Chaitanya Sir's room before first bell and showed him the screenshots. "This is not your fault," Chaitanya Sir said, and stayed beside Jatin while calling the school's safeguarding lead. She arrived within the hour, copied the screenshots and said the school would deal with the sharing. Jatin blocked the accounts and reported the post.
The following Monday the photo was gone, the safeguarding lead had checked in twice, and Jatin ate lunch with two classmates.

qa.q: What did Jatin do with the photo and the names before putting the phone away?
qa.a: Jatin took screenshots of the photo and the names.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel when finding the photo, and what shows it?
qa.a: Exposed and helpless; the cold hands and the wish to disappear show it, and Jatin did not reply.

qa.q: Which step turned things around, and why?
qa.a: Showing the screenshots to Chaitanya Sir before first bell, because an adult could reassure Jatin and pass it to the safeguarding lead the same day.

qa.q: What might Chaitanya Sir have seen in Jatin walking in that early?
qa.a: A student who was upset but brave enough to ask for help, which is why Chaitanya Sir stayed close and said it was not Jatin's fault.

grounding: A teenager finds a photo shared with cruel comments and uses evidence, a trusted adult, reporting and blocking.

passage: Gurpreet, put the phone down a minute. When I was fifteen there was a clip of me falling off the stage at our school farewell, and an older class shared it with laughing comments. My face burned as if the whole town had watched. My hands shook, but I remembered to save pictures of the comments before doing anything else. Then I told my mother, standing in the kitchen with the phone still in my hand. She hugged me first and said it was in no way my fault. That same evening she phoned the principal, who listened, took the pictures I had saved and promised action. By the next day the clip was down, and I had blocked those accounts. I still remember how light I felt walking into school after. Nandini

qa.q: What did Nandini fall off at the school farewell?
qa.a: Nandini fell off the stage at the school farewell.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel on seeing the clip, and what shows it?
qa.a: Ashamed and exposed; the burning face and the shaking hands show it.

qa.q: What did young Nandini do before anything else, and why did it help?
qa.a: Nandini saved pictures of the comments first, which gave the principal proof to act on.

qa.q: How might Nandini's mother have felt hearing the news in the kitchen?
qa.a: Worried and protective; hugging first and saying it was not Nandini's fault shows care before action.

grounding: A teenager finds a clip shared with cruel comments and saves evidence, tells a trusted adult, and the school acts.

passage: I'm Omkar, Harsha's roommate in the hostel, and I notice things at night. Around eleven Harsha lies down with the phone held above the face, thumbs sliding. I catch glimpses: a classmate on a beach, a cousin's wedding, someone's offer letter. The sighs get longer. Last night Harsha said, "Everyone is moving ahead and I'm standing here." I don't know what was going on inside that head, only that the mood dropped. I said those pictures were the best ten seconds of a person's week. Harsha snorted but did not argue. This morning I found a daily limit set on the phone and the phone on the shelf, and we went to the canteen for breakfast without it.

qa.q: Where do Omkar and Harsha live together?
qa.a: Omkar and Harsha are roommates in the hostel.

qa.q: What might Harsha be feeling as the sighs get longer, and how sure can Omkar be?
qa.a: Behind and discouraged, judging by the sighs and the remark about everyone moving ahead, but Omkar admits not knowing what was going on inside.

qa.q: What small step did Harsha take, and why might it help?
qa.a: Setting a daily limit and putting the phone on the shelf, because less scrolling means fewer highlight reels to compare with.

qa.q: Why might Omkar have called the pictures the best ten seconds of a person's week?
qa.a: To remind Harsha gently that posts show highlights, not whole lives, without lecturing.

grounding: A young adult scrolls through friends' milestones and feels behind, then limits phone time.

passage:
Sunday night. Francis scrolled for an hour through friends' holidays, a wedding in Goa and Riya's new job, and felt like the only person standing still. Sleep came late.
Tuesday. In the canteen Mohit showed the holiday photos and laughed, "You should have seen the bus breakdown and the two-hour argument about money." Francis realised the pictures showed the sunset, not the argument.
Saturday. Francis set a daily limit on the phone, muted two accounts that made the chest go tight, and spent the afternoon at the cricket nets with Mohit. The next Sunday there was still some scrolling, but only ten minutes of it, and breakfast felt lighter.

qa.q: What did Mohit say happened on the holiday besides the sunset?
qa.a: Mohit mentioned the bus breakdown and the two-hour argument about money.

qa.q: What did Francis feel on Sunday night?
qa.a: Left behind; an hour of holidays, a wedding and a job announcement made Francis feel like the only person standing still.

qa.q: Which changes helped Francis's mood?
qa.a: Setting a daily limit and muting two accounts, plus spending time in person with Mohit.

qa.q: How might the holiday photos look from Mohit's side?
qa.a: Mohit remembers the whole trip, including the breakdown and the argument, so the photos are only the pleasant part.

grounding: A young adult feels behind after friends' posts, learns they show highlights only, and limits scrolling.

passage: Elizabeth read the message twice on the metro to college: a white van was taking children near schools, and it said forward to everyone you love. Her heart pounded. She sent it to the family group before the next station. By evening her aunt had phoned three neighbours and told the twin cousins not to walk to the park. Aparna, Elizabeth's cousin, texted privately: "Where did this come from? The photo looks old." Elizabeth's face went hot. She searched and found the same picture from another city years ago, with no local report at all. She deleted her forward, wrote "Sorry, I didn't check. Please ignore it," and phoned her aunt to explain.

qa.q: When did Elizabeth send the message to the family group?
qa.a: Elizabeth sent it before the next station.

qa.q: Why did Elizabeth forward the message without checking?
qa.a: Fear made it feel urgent; the pounding heart and the line about forwarding to everyone loved made Elizabeth act at once.

qa.q: What could Elizabeth do before forwarding a shocking message next time?
qa.a: Pause, check where it came from and whether any local report exists, and skip the forward if not.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth's aunt have felt after phoning three neighbours?
qa.a: Worried, and then perhaps embarrassed once Elizabeth explained, because the panic had already spread.

grounding: A young adult forwards a shocking message to the family group unchecked, then learns to pause and check the source.

passage:
Kavitha: Damini, your Nani just phoned me in tears. She says the college is shutting for a week because of some threat.
Damini: Oh no. I forwarded that to the family group last night. It looked official.
Kavitha: Who wrote it?
Damini: I... it just said forward to everyone. No name.
Kavitha: Is there a notice on the college website?
Damini: Checking. Nothing. And the class group says lectures are normal.
Kavitha: So what now?
Damini: I'll delete it and write to the family, "That message was false, sorry, please ignore." And I'll ring Nani myself.
Kavitha: Good. Next time, check first.

qa.q: What did the message say would happen to the college?
qa.a: It said the college is shutting for a week because of some threat.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when forwarding the message to the family group?
qa.a: Damini was probably worried for the family, since the message looked official and important, so forwarding felt protective; Damini did not check who wrote it.

qa.q: What did Damini do to put things right?
qa.a: Checked the college website and class group, deleted the forward, told the family it was false and rang Nani.

qa.q: What is it like for Nani when a shocking false message arrives?
qa.a: Frightening; Nani was in tears on the phone before anyone knew whether it was true.

grounding: A young adult forwards a shocking message in a family group, then checks the source and corrects it.

passage: I'm Wasim, and I sit opposite Sonali at work. At lunch Sonali was scrolling through a clip of a woman shouting at a shop clerk, with thousands of comments calling for her to be sacked and shamed. I watched Sonali type a comment, stare at it and delete it. Twice. Then Sonali said, "It's thirty seconds. What happened before?" and spent the rest of the break searching. A longer video turned up: the clerk had been curt for several minutes, and the woman was holding a crying child. Neither looked like the villain of a thirty-second clip. Sonali closed the app and posted nothing. I can't say what was in Sonali's mind, but the face looked tired, not angry.

qa.q: How long was the clip Sonali first saw?
qa.a: The clip was thirty seconds.

qa.q: What might Sonali have felt when typing and deleting the comment, and how sure can Wasim be?
qa.a: Pulled to join in but uneasy about it; Wasim only saw the typing and deleting and cannot be sure of Sonali's mind.

qa.q: What did Sonali do that was fair, and what could follow?
qa.a: Sonali looked for the earlier part and posted nothing, and could also decline to share the clip.

qa.q: How might the woman in the clip feel about thousands of comments?
qa.a: Humiliated and afraid, especially since her holding a crying child was missing from the short clip.

grounding: A user watches thousands attack a person over a clip, feels the pull to join, and refuses to add cruelty.

passage:
Monday. A clip of a man arguing with a bus conductor spread across every feed. By evening there were tens of thousands of comments demanding that the man lose his job. Sonali typed, "People like this should be..." then stopped, thumb hovering. She put the phone face down.
Wednesday. Siddharth from the next desk showed her a longer video: the fare dispute had run for ten minutes, and both men had raised their voices. Sonali felt relieved she had not posted.
Friday. Another clip trended. Sonali scrolled past, then messaged Siddharth: "Waiting for the full story this time." Siddharth wrote back, "Same."

qa.q: How many comments were there by Monday evening?
qa.a: There were tens of thousands of comments.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling while the thumb hovered over the comment?
qa.a: Tempted and uneasy; the pull to join the crowd met a doubt about adding cruelty.

qa.q: What did Sonali do differently on Friday?
qa.a: Sonali scrolled past the new clip and decided to wait for the full story.

qa.q: How might the man in the clip feel about the flood of comments?
qa.a: Exposed and frightened, since people demanded he lose his job while the longer video showed both men raising their voices.

grounding: A user feels the pull to join a pile-on, then sees the story was partial and refuses to add cruelty.

passage: Two hours before the application portal closed, Varun sat on a delayed train with his phone at fifteen per cent and one bar of signal, polishing his public profile. He had typed "visionary leader" and "award-winning" over a college quiz he had co-won. His sister Shreya called. "Why do you sound like a brochure?" Varun laughed, uneasy. He read it back and felt like an actor. He cut the puffed-up words and wrote what he had actually done: led a four-person project, co-won a state quiz. He kept the good photo. The cooking pictures stayed in the private account that only close friends could see. He submitted with a minute to spare.

qa.q: What did Shreya ask when she called?
qa.a: Shreya asked, Why do you sound like a brochure?

qa.q: How did Varun feel reading the profile back, and why?
qa.a: Like an actor; uneasy because the puffed-up words were not what Varun had actually done.

qa.q: Which choices kept the profile honest but still polished?
qa.a: Cutting the inflated words, stating what Varun had actually done and keeping the cooking pictures private.

qa.q: Why might Shreya have made the brochure remark?
qa.a: Shreya heard that the profile did not sound like Varun and joked gently to nudge honesty.

grounding: A young professional curates a public image, feels the strain of performing, and stays honest while keeping private space.

passage: In the Kolkata office lift, Yusuf overheard Arnab muttering a caption. "Led the whole campaign," it said. Arnab had actually built one of three parts. Every evening Arnab posted a polished update, and lately the effort felt like a second job: checking reactions before dinner and going to bed feeling flat. Yusuf said lightly, "You're better than your captions." Arnab thought about that all the way home. That night the caption became "Built the email part of a team campaign," and the post got fewer likes. Arnab felt lighter anyway. The weekend photos moved to a separate account with just a few close friends.

qa.q: How many parts of the campaign had Arnab actually built?
qa.a: Arnab had built one of three parts.

qa.q: How did Arnab feel about the daily posting, and what shows it?
qa.a: Strained; the effort felt like a second job and Arnab went to bed feeling flat.

qa.q: Which changes kept Arnab's image honest and protected privacy?
qa.a: Rewriting the caption to say exactly what Arnab did and moving weekend photos to a separate account for close friends.

qa.q: What might Yusuf have meant by You're better than your captions?
qa.a: That Arnab's real work was good enough and did not need exaggeration, said kindly and briefly.

grounding: A young professional curates a public image, feels the strain, and returns to honest captions and a private circle.

passage: Thursday, 10 pm. Small wins today. From seven to eight the phone stayed in the drawer, and dinner tasted like actual food. I muted three accounts that leave me feeling behind, and nothing exploded. I kept the office group and the family group, because I need those. Santosh from the next desk laughed when I said I'd try a phone-free lunch, but joined me anyway and we walked to the tea stall. It's odd how loud my own thoughts were at first. By the end of lunch they were just thoughts. Tomorrow: the phone charges outside the bedroom. Ganga

qa.q: Which two groups did Ganga keep?
qa.a: Ganga kept the office group and the family group.

qa.q: Why did Ganga mute three accounts, and how did it feel?
qa.a: The accounts left Ganga feeling behind; muting them brought calm, since nothing exploded.

qa.q: What small step is planned for tomorrow?
qa.a: The phone will charge outside the bedroom.

qa.q: How might Santosh have felt about the phone-free lunch after laughing?
qa.a: A little doubtful at first, then relaxed and happy to chat, since Santosh came along anyway.

grounding: A young adult chooses phone-free times, mutes draining accounts and keeps useful groups and real-life company.

passage:
Jyoti: Guess what, I've muted the two accounts that make me feel behind 🙂
Jahnavi: Wait, both? Even Meera's holiday page?
Jyoti: Even that. I kept her messages, just not the posts.
Jahnavi: And the phone at night?
Jyoti: In the kitchen from nine. I read a real book and I'm asleep by ten 😴
Jahnavi: Okay, you've made me curious. Tea on Saturday at my place, no phones on the table?
Jyoti: Deal. I'm keeping the class group on though, I need those notes.
Jahnavi: Obviously. See you at four!

qa.q: Where does Jyoti keep the phone from nine at night?
qa.a: Jyoti keeps the phone in the kitchen from nine.

qa.q: How does Jyoti feel about the muted accounts, and why?
qa.a: Calmer and lighter, because the accounts made Jyoti feel behind.

qa.q: Which boundary keeps a useful connection?
qa.a: Keeping the class group on, since the notes are needed.

qa.q: How does Jahnavi react to the changes?
qa.a: Curious and interested, and invites Jyoti for tea with no phones on the table.

grounding: A young adult mutes draining accounts, keeps the phone away at night and plans an in-person tea, while keeping a useful group.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: Two-year-old Abhinav had spent a year abroad, where visitors kept an arm's length. Now, on the veranda of his grandparents' village home, aunts swooped in, pinching cheeks and passing him around. His mouth went tight, his fists pushed at hands, and he shouted "No!" His mother, Aditi, saw his eyes searching for her face. "Give him a minute," she said, lifting him onto her hip. He rested his head on her shoulder, then reached one finger toward an aunt's bangle.

qa.q: Where did the aunts pass Abhinav around?
qa.a: They passed Abhinav around on the veranda of his grandparents' village home.

qa.q: What did Aditi seem to want for Abhinav, and what did Aditi notice?
qa.a: Aditi wanted Abhinav to feel safe and unhurried, and noticed the eyes searching for her face.

qa.q: What choice by Aditi helped Abhinav settle?
qa.a: Lifting Abhinav onto her hip and giving a minute, so that the touch of the bangle came in Abhinav's own time.

qa.q: What might Abhinav have been feeling when passed around?
qa.a: Overwhelmed and cross; the tight mouth, pushing fists and shouted No show it.

grounding: A toddler shows discomfort at being passed between strangers' arms, and a parent reads the cue and responds.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: In Lisbon, Great-Aunt Rosa scooped up eighteen-month-old Zanele and kissed both cheeks. Zanele giggled and patted her face. Days later in Helsinki, cousins smiled and waved from an arm's length and did not touch. Zanele frowned, held both arms up, whined, then threw a spoon. Hana, Zanele's mother, watched the little eyes go from face to face, checking each adult's stillness. Hana lifted Zanele for a cuddle, and one cousin waved slowly and offered a toy.

qa.q: Where did the cousins wave from?
qa.a: The cousins waved from an arm's length.

qa.q: What did Hana seem to realise from watching Zanele's eyes go from face to face?
qa.a: That Zanele was reading each adult's comfort, checking for stillness or warmth before deciding how to act.

qa.q: What did Hana do that helped, and what did a cousin add?
qa.a: Hana lifted Zanele for a cuddle, and one cousin waved slowly and offered a toy.

qa.q: How did Zanele react differently in Helsinki than in Lisbon?
qa.a: Zanele giggled with Great-Aunt Rosa but frowned, whined and threw a spoon when kept at arm's length, perhaps missing touch.

grounding: A toddler is held by strangers in one place and kept apart in another and reacts to each; a caregiver notices.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: The corridor outside Class 5 was roaring before the bell, and Anand Sir had five minutes to find out whose pencil box was left open. He asked Parveen, "Did you see it? Eyes on me while I am talking." Parveen's eyes stayed on the floor. At home, Dadi always said that meeting an elder's eyes is rude. Anand Sir's voice sharpened, and Parveen's throat closed. Then the bell rang and the noise faded. Anand Sir crouched and asked, "Tell me why you look down." Parveen explained. "In my class, looking at me shows you're listening," said Anand Sir. "At home, looking down shows respect. Both are kind." They agreed on a quick glance at the start, then a nod.

qa.q: What did Dadi always say to Parveen?
qa.a: Dadi always said that meeting an elder's eyes is rude.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling when the teacher asked for eye contact?
qa.a: Frightened and stuck; Parveen's throat closed and the eyes stayed on the floor out of respect.

qa.q: What could help Parveen and Anand Sir understand each other next time?
qa.a: A quick glance at the start and then a nod, which they agreed together.

qa.q: How might Anand Sir have read Parveen's lowered eyes at first?
qa.a: As not listening or hiding something, until Parveen explained it was respect.

grounding: A child taught not to meet an elder's eyes meets a teacher who asks for eye contact, and patient translation follows.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: On the morning of the school science fair, Dhruv practised the talk in front of Manjula Ma'am in a Mumbai classroom. Dhruv spoke to the floor. "Look at the judges, Dhruv," said Manjula Ma'am. "It shows confidence." Dhruv's voice shrank. Later, at the dinner table, Dhruv told Mummy. "Nani says looking straight at an elder is bad manners." Mummy thought and said, "At home Nani is right for us. On the stage, Ma'am is right for the judges. You are learning two ways of showing respect." The next day Dhruv looked at the judges for a moment, then at the model, then again at the judges, and won a small ribbon.

qa.q: Where did Dhruv practise the talk?
qa.a: Dhruv practised in front of Manjula Ma'am in a classroom.

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel when Manjula Ma'am asked for eye contact, and why?
qa.a: Uncomfortable and torn; the voice shrank because looking at adults felt rude at home.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that helped Dhruv?
qa.a: Mummy explained that both Nani and Ma'am are right in their own places, so Dhruv could use each without shame.

qa.q: How does Manjula Ma'am see eye contact on the stage?
qa.a: As a sign of confidence in front of the judges.

grounding: A child taught that looking an elder in the eye is rude meets a teacher who wants eye contact, and an adult translates.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: Pallavi had been back in Pune from her exchange term in Utrecht for a week when she watched her classmate Jagdish invite her aunt to a birthday. "Maybe, we'll see," said her aunt with a warm smile. Jagdish nodded happily and said he would keep a chair. Pallavi bit her lip: at home a soft maybe is sometimes a gentle no. In Utrecht her host family had said, "No, I don't want to," straight out, and at first she had felt slapped. Now she saw that neither was rude in its own place. She quietly told Jagdish, "Maybe can be a kind way of saying no. You could ask her again another way." Jagdish laughed and thanked her.

qa.q: Where had Pallavi spent her exchange term?
qa.a: Pallavi spent her exchange term in Utrecht.

qa.q: What did Pallavi feel when her aunt said maybe, and why?
qa.a: Uneasy and a little worried for Jagdish, because a warm maybe can be a gentle no, and Pallavi had just learned the bluntness abroad.

qa.q: How could Pallavi help Jagdish read both styles?
qa.a: By explaining that maybe can be a kind way of saying no and suggesting he ask again another way, without calling either style rude.

qa.q: How might Jagdish have felt hearing maybe, we'll see?
qa.a: Hopeful and happy, taking the warm smile as a likely yes.

grounding: A teenager on exchange notices direct and indirect refusals and sees neither is rude in its own setting.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage:
In the school canteen in Auckland, Chinmay tried something new.
Chinmay: Nilesh, do you want to come to the night market with me tonight?
Nilesh: No, thanks. I'm going to stay in and finish my project.
Chinmay: Oh. Okay. (The smile slid for a second.)
Nilesh: What? Did I say something wrong?
Chinmay: At home a no usually comes wrapped in a maybe. Like, let me see.
Nilesh: Here, if I mean maybe I say maybe. If I mean no I say no. It isn't rude.
Chinmay: I'm starting to see that. So can I ask what you'd like to do on Saturday?
Nilesh: Saturday, yes! Table tennis?
Chinmay: Table tennis. And if you're tired, just tell me straight.
Nilesh: Deal.

qa.q: What plan did Nilesh give instead of going to the night market?
qa.a: Nilesh planned to stay in and finish the project.

qa.q: How did Chinmay feel at first on hearing No, thanks?
qa.a: A little hurt or taken aback; the smile slid for a second.

qa.q: How did Chinmay handle the difference next?
qa.a: Chinmay asked Nilesh about Saturday and asked for straight answers when Nilesh is tired.

qa.q: Why does Nilesh say a no is not rude?
qa.a: Because in that place maybe means maybe and no means no, so being direct is honest, not unkind.

grounding: A teenager on exchange notices that a blunt no abroad differs from a softened maybe at home and learns to read both.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: At the tea stall in Nagaur, Harish stood shoulder to shoulder with Deepak, talking the way people do in a small town where everyone stands close. It reminded Harish of the internship in Stuttgart. There, Harish had stood a hand's width from a colleague, chatting eagerly, and the colleague had taken one step back, then another. Harish felt rejected and wondered what had been said wrong. Weeks later a co-intern explained that some people there like a wider gap, and that it was comfort, not dislike. "So I started noticing," Harish told Deepak, "who leans in and who steps away." Harish moved half a step back, just to try. Deepak laughed and stepped in closer, and they both grinned.

qa.q: Where did Harish's internship take place?
qa.a: The internship was in Stuttgart.

qa.q: How did Harish feel when the colleague stepped back?
qa.a: Rejected and confused, wondering what had been said wrong.

qa.q: What did Harish learn to do afterwards?
qa.a: Notice who leans in and who steps away, and adjust the distance.

qa.q: How might Deepak see Harish moving half a step back?
qa.a: As a funny experiment, since Deepak laughed and stepped in closer.

grounding: A young adult who stood close to a colleague abroad felt rejected, then learned about different comfort distances.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: On her third day at the design studio in Helsinki, Aiko leaned in beside Xin to look at a drawing, close enough to smell the tea. Xin took a small step back. Aiko stepped forward again. Xin stepped back again, and Aiko's cheeks went hot. Rejected, Aiko ate lunch alone and wondered what had gone wrong. That afternoon a note from the placement guide mentioned that people differ in how much space feels comfortable. Aiko asked Xin, "Am I standing too close?" Xin smiled. "A little. It's not about you, I just like room." After that Aiko kept an arm's length, and Xin began to lean in first when sharing sketches.

qa.q: What did Xin do when Aiko leaned in?
qa.a: Xin took a small step back.

qa.q: How did Aiko feel at lunch, and why?
qa.a: Rejected and confused; Aiko's cheeks had gone hot and Aiko ate alone wondering what had gone wrong.

qa.q: What did Aiko do that turned it around?
qa.a: Asked Xin openly whether Aiko was standing too close, then kept an arm's length.

qa.q: What is it like for Xin when someone stands very close?
qa.a: Uncomfortable, since Xin likes room, but Xin says it is not about Aiko personally.

grounding: A young adult standing close sees a colleague step back, feels rejected, and learns about different comfort distances.
